\chapter{Five Words for What a Thing Is Worth}
\label{ch:importante-y-facil}
\hlchaptermodality{398}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say importante, interesante, favorito, fácil and difícil, and say what I think of something.}

Complete ES-C398-dificil: say what you think of five things, and why.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[importante]{importante — what a thing carries in with it}

\label{lesson:ES-C398-importante}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{bigger, older}, then \emph{smaller, younger}. (\emph{Mayor}; \emph{menor}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la puerta — the same \emph{port-} you are about to meet.
  \item el precio — one thing that can matter.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{im-por-TAN-te}, four beats with the weight on the third. Every vowel stays short and clean — none of them slides. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{importante} — \textquotedblleft{}important.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart and it is \emph{importar} with an \emph{-ante} on the end. And \emph{importar} is Latin \textbf{importāre}: \textbf{in-} + \textbf{portāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{carry in}.\textquotedblright{}

That is all it meant in Latin. Bring in. Introduce. Bring about. A Roman who said \emph{importat} was talking about cargo, not significance.

So where did \emph{mattering} come from? Later, and not from Rome. The sense grew up inside the Romance languages after Latin, and the dictionaries that follow the trail point at \textbf{Italian} as the place it started. Spanish and French both have it; Latin did not. This is one of the cases where the modern meaning is younger than the word by a thousand years.

English kept both jobs in one word, which is the clearest way to see it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to \textbf{import} goods} — to carry them in;
  \item \emph{the \textbf{import} of his remarks} — their weight, what they bring in with them.
\end{itemize}

Same word, both senses, sitting in an English dictionary right now.

The \emph{portāre} family is large and you will recognise all of it: \textbf{portable}, \textbf{porter}, \textbf{transport}, \textbf{export}, \textbf{report}, \textbf{deport}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Es muy \textbf{importante}}. — It is very important.
  \item \emph{No \textbf{importa}}. — It does not matter.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing matters: \emph{importante}. And you know that the mattering is the new part — the old part is nothing but carrying something in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{importante}
  \item \emph{es muy importante}
  \item \emph{no importa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{importāre} mean? (\emph{To carry in} — nothing about mattering.) Which English word still does both jobs at once? (\emph{Import}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[interesante]{interesante — what stands between you and it}

\label{lesson:ES-C398-interesante}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{smaller, younger}, then \emph{important}. (\emph{Menor}; \emph{importante}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item importante — its neighbour, built the same way.
  \item el dinero — you will need it for the second half of this.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{in-te-re-SAN-te}, five beats with the weight on the fourth. Every \emph{e} is the same short, flat vowel — none of them drifts toward English \emph{uh}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{interesante} — \textquotedblleft{}interesting.\textquotedblright{}

Underneath is Latin \textbf{interesse}: \textbf{inter} (\textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{esse} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}). \emph{To be between.}

The step from there to \emph{interesting} is short. What stands \textbf{between} you and something else is what concerns you, what you have a stake in. Spanish keeps the plain verb — \emph{interesar}, \textquotedblleft{}to interest\textquotedblright{} — and the noun \emph{interés}.

\textbf{And now the good part, which is about money.}

Medieval canon law forbade charging for a loan; that was usury. But it permitted a lender to recover what he had \emph{lost by not having his money} — and lawyers named that \textbf{id quod interest}: \textquotedblleft{}that which is between.\textquotedblright{} The difference between where the lender stood and where he would have stood.

The prohibition is long gone. The name stayed. Every time a bank quotes you an \textbf{interest} rate, it is using a Latin lawyer's phrase for a gap.

Spanish holds the same double:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un libro \textbf{interesante}} — an interesting book;
  \item \emph{el \textbf{interés} del banco} — the bank's interest.
\end{itemize}

The \emph{esse} half turns up in English too, in \textbf{essence} and \textbf{present} — the verb \emph{to be}, dressed differently each time.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing holds your attention: \emph{interesante}. And you know why a bank's charge and your curiosity are the same word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{interesante}
  \item \emph{un libro interesante}
  \item \emph{muy interesante}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{inter} and \emph{esse} mean apart? (\emph{Between}, and \emph{to be}.) What were medieval lenders allowed to recover, since they could not charge for a loan? (\emph{Id quod interest} — the difference, \textquotedblleft{}that which is between.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[favorito]{favorito — an ending that only looks like a little word}

\label{lesson:ES-C398-favorito}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{important}, then \emph{interesting}. (\emph{Importante}; \emph{interesante}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — and the \emph{casita} you can make from it. Hold that ending.
  \item el color — what you will use this word about.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fa-vo-RI-to}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{v} is the same soft sound as Spanish \emph{b}, made with both lips. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{favorito} — \textquotedblleft{}favourite.\textquotedblright{}

The root is easy. \textbf{Favor} is Latin \textbf{favēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be well disposed toward, to look kindly on.\textquotedblright{} English has \textbf{favour}, \textbf{favourable}, and — from the same verb — the \textbf{fan}, who is a \emph{favourer} of a team.

\textbf{Now look at the ending, because it is a trap.}

You have met \emph{-ito} before. It is the ending that turns \emph{casa} into \emph{casita}, a little house. Seeing \emph{favor} + \emph{-ito}, a reader who has learned that ending will read \textquotedblleft{}a little favour.\textquotedblright{}

It is not that ending.

\emph{Favorito} was borrowed whole from Italian \textbf{favorito} — and in Italian, that is the \textbf{past participle} of the verb \emph{favorire}. It means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}favoured.\textquotedblright{}} The \emph{-ito} was already on the word when Spanish took it; nobody in Spanish added it. Two endings that look identical, doing entirely different work, and only the word's history tells them apart.

English took the very same Italian word by the same road, through French, in the 1500s — so \textbf{favourite} and \emph{favorito} are the same borrowing twice over.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mi color \textbf{favorito}} — my favourite colour;
  \item \emph{mi comida \textbf{favorita}} — my favourite food.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the one you like best: \emph{favorito}. And you have seen two identical endings that mean different things — one Spanish and small, one Italian and participial.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{favorito}
  \item \emph{mi color favorito}
  \item \emph{mi comida favorita}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the \emph{-ito} of \emph{favorito} mean \textquotedblleft{}little\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{No} — it is an Italian past participle meaning \emph{favoured}, and it arrived already attached.) What does Latin \emph{favēre} mean? (\emph{To look kindly on}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fácil]{fácil — not \textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}, but \textquotedblleft{}doable\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C398-facil}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{interesting}, then \emph{favourite}. (\emph{Interesante}; \emph{favorito}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hacer — you already own this. It is about to turn out to be the same word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FÁ-cil}, two beats with the weight on the first — and the written accent is there to tell you so. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fácil} — \textquotedblleft{}easy.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{facilis} is \textbf{facere}, \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} with an ending that means \emph{-able}.

So the word does not say \emph{light}. It does not say \emph{gentle}. It says \textbf{doable}. That is a sharper idea than \textquotedblleft{}easy,\textquotedblright{} and a kinder one: a thing is \emph{fácil} because you can do it.

\textbf{And you have met \emph{facere} already.} It is \emph{hacer}.

Look at the two side by side:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{hacer}} — carried in the mouth for centuries. The \emph{f} fell away to an \emph{h} that nobody pronounces, and the middle softened out entirely.
  \item \emph{\textbf{fácil}} — lifted off a Latin page long afterwards, by people reading. It still shows the \emph{f} and the \emph{c}, because it had no journey in which to lose them.
\end{itemize}

One Latin verb, two arrivals, and the spelling of each records how it travelled.

The bookish end of the family is all in English: \textbf{facile}, \textbf{facility}, \textbf{faculty}. And a \emph{facility} is exactly what the Latin says — a thing that makes something \textbf{doable}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Es muy \textbf{fácil}}. — It is very easy.
  \item \emph{un examen \textbf{fácil}} — an easy exam.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing gives no trouble: \emph{fácil}. And you can hear \emph{hacer} inside it — the same verb, arriving twice by two different roads.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fácil}
  \item \emph{es muy fácil}
  \item \emph{hacer, fácil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{facilis} say a thing is, literally? (\emph{Doable} — \emph{facere} plus an \emph{-able} ending.) Which verb you already know is the same Latin word? (\emph{Hacer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[difícil]{difícil — the word English had to build backwards}

\label{lesson:ES-C398-dificil}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{favourite}, then \emph{easy}. (\emph{Favorito}; \emph{fácil}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item fácil — this word is that word with a \emph{no} on the front.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{di-FÍ-cil}, three beats with the weight on the middle one, which the written accent marks. Both \emph{c} and the second \emph{i} stay soft and short. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{difícil} — \textquotedblleft{}difficult.\textquotedblright{}

You already have the whole word. Latin \textbf{difficilis} is \textbf{dis-} — the prefix that undoes things — stuck on \textbf{facilis}.

\textbf{Not doable.}

That is the entire construction, and it is worth saying aloud in that order: \emph{facilis}, doable; \emph{difficilis}, not doable. Latin doubled the letter when \emph{dis-} ran into that \emph{f}, which is why the Latin has \emph{-ff-}, and Spanish later settled back to one.

\textbf{The strange half of this story is English, not Spanish.}

English did not borrow \emph{difficult} as an adjective. It borrowed the \textbf{noun} first — \textbf{difficulty}, from Latin \emph{difficultās} — and then, about a century later, writers cut the adjective \emph{back out of it}. \textbf{Difficult} is a word made by trimming a longer word that was already there.

So Spanish holds the plain inherited shape, and English holds one that had to be reverse-engineered. When you say \emph{difícil}, you are saying the older, simpler thing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Es \textbf{difícil}}. — It is difficult.
  \item \emph{un examen \textbf{difícil}} — a hard exam.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say a thing gives trouble: \emph{difícil}. You have five words for saying what you think of something — \emph{importante}, \emph{interesante}, \emph{favorito}, \emph{fácil}, \emph{difícil} — and you can build the last one out of the one before it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{difícil}
  \item \emph{fácil, difícil}
  \item \emph{un examen difícil}
  \item \emph{importante, interesante, favorito, fácil, difícil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Take \emph{difícil} apart. (\emph{Dis-} plus \emph{facilis} — \textquotedblleft{}not doable.\textquotedblright{}) Which came into English first, \emph{difficult} or \emph{difficulty}? (\emph{Difficulty} — the adjective was cut out of the noun afterwards.)
\end{tcolorbox}
